doc.title: Dave Rivello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Prospects for young jazz graduates
summary: He says prospects are poor but passion and entrepreneurial skills, such as Eastman's Arts Leadership Program, help.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: If Eastman — I don’t know how many jazz majors graduate from Eastman every year, but if you multiply that times the number of universities in the country now who are doing similar work, what’s the prospect for a young talented musician with a degree, in the business?

Not too good, to be honest. And I think about that. Because I think not only in music but even say you have a degree in painting. Where are you going to go? You know, you have a degree in poetry. What are you going to do? You know, Starbucks? Hey. But I do believe that with passion and commitment and energy, those people, the ones that are that dedicated, will rise to someplace where they can do their art and make a living. It’s a difficult thing because there isn’t too much of a place in our society, and with budget cuts and everything else, there’s just — so everybody has to find their own way. I think, that’s why I take the pedagogy class so seriously. Because I feel that with community colleges, even if somebody is not a music education major, they’re a jazz major, but there might be an improvisation class that they could pick up on Tuesday nights in whatever town they’re in, or an adult education improvisation class, or something that they can do that will help supplement the music that they want to create. So finding ways — that’s why I’m happy that Eastman has the Arts Leadership Program, and so a lot of that seems to be teaching musicians how to create their own gigs, how to get people to show up to those gigs, and so basically, entrepreneurial skills. Because I think that’s what’s necessary today. It’s not just the same way it was where, okay, so I play good and I’m getting hired by Woody Herman’s band, and I’m good for a while, and eventually maybe I get tired of that so I play with somebody else for a while, and then I’ll get a job teaching college in the town that I settle in. We don’t have any of that. So finding ways, creative ways, I
think it’s necessary now for musicians to find creative ways to make a living and still stay true to their art.
